title: Ladder Setup, Stability, and Traffic Control

content.overview: A sound ladder can still become hazardous when it is placed on an unstable surface, set where a door or cart can strike it, or used without fully engaging its designed support system. Setup converts inspected equipment into a safe or unsafe work station. Cultivation workers must account for floors, drainage, irrigation, carts, rolling benches, doorways, crop traffic, and changing work conditions before climbing.

vocabulary.definition: A supporting surface that can hold the ladder without shifting, sinking, rocking, or unexpected movement during intended use.
Barriers, routing, communication, or access controls used to prevent people, carts, doors, or equipment from contacting the ladder setup.
The floor and surrounding space that must remain controlled for ladder footing, access, and worker movement.

sections.title: Control the base and support
sections.body: Portable ladders should be placed on stable and level surfaces unless the ladder is secured or stabilized as allowed by the applicable requirement. Before use, clear hoses, loose debris, standing liquid, movable containers, and other conditions that can affect footing. For a stepladder, fully open and engage the designed spreader or locking system. Never substitute blocks, stacked materials, or another person for a stable setup.

sections.title: Protect the setup from movement around it
sections.body: A ladder beside a door, cart lane, rolling bench, harvest tote route, or busy aisle can be destabilized by someone who is not part of the task. Control the area before climbing. Depending on the workplace, this may mean locking or guarding a door, using a barrier, temporarily rerouting traffic, assigning a spotter for traffic control, or rescheduling work. A spotter can help control the environment but does not convert defective equipment or an improper setup into a safe one.

sections.title: Reassess when conditions change
sections.body: Setup is not a one-time decision. Irrigation may start, a floor may become wet, carts may arrive, lighting equipment may move, or another crew may enter the area. If the original controlled conditions no longer exist, descend safely and reset the task. OSHA also prohibits moving, shifting, or extending a ladder while it is occupied. Repositioning requires the worker to get down and establish the new setup before climbing again.

workedExamples: A step ladder is needed near a propagation-room doorway. The worker coordinates access, keeps the door from opening into the ladder zone, establishes a visible barrier, confirms the floor is dry, and then climbs.
While a worker is elevated, irrigation creates water near one ladder foot. The correct response is to descend and correct the condition, not to finish quickly before the puddle grows.
commonMistakes: Assuming a level-looking floor is stable without clearing liquid, hoses, debris, or movable objects.
Using a spotter as a substitute for proper equipment condition or setup.
Trying to scoot or shift a ladder while someone remains on it.
content.practicalApplication: Lay out a simulated ladder setup in a cultivation aisle. Mark the setup zone, identify at least four ways the surrounding workflow could destabilize it, and specify the barrier, routing, scheduling, or stop-work control for each hazard.
content.summary: Ladder stability depends on both the equipment and the environment around it. Control the footing, engage the ladder as designed, protect the setup from traffic, and reset the job whenever conditions change.
